title: Revenue
formula: Revenue = Core sales + Client revenue + B2B sales + Expansion revenue
meaning: Revenue is the value of sales earned during the period before deducting costs.
higherLower: Higher revenue is useful only when margins and cash economics remain healthy.
simpleExample: If a shop earns $8,000 from normal sales and $2,000 from a corporate order, total revenue is $10,000.

title: Direct / Variable Costs
formula: Variable costs = Core COGS + Client variable costs + Sales-contract variable costs
meaning: These are costs that rise mainly because the company sold or delivered more.
higherLower: Lower variable cost per unit generally improves margins, but cutting quality can hurt retention and demand.
simpleExample: If 1,000 units cost $4 each to deliver, variable costs are $4,000.

title: Gross Profit
formula: Gross profit = Revenue − Variable costs
meaning: Gross profit is the money left from sales after paying direct costs, before overhead such as payroll, rent and marketing.
higherLower: Higher gross profit gives the business more capacity to pay operating expenses and reinvest.

title: Gross Margin
formula: Gross margin % = Gross profit ÷ Revenue × 100
meaning: Gross margin shows how much of each revenue dollar remains after direct costs.
higherLower: A higher margin usually provides more operating cushion, but normal margins vary greatly by industry.

title: Operating Expenses
formula: Operating expenses = Fixed + Discretionary + Payroll + One-time expenses + Asset maintenance
meaning: Operating expenses are the costs of running the company beyond direct production or delivery.
higherLower: Lower is not automatically better; underinvesting in people, product or marketing can reduce future growth.

title: Operating Profit
formula: Operating profit = Gross profit − Operating expenses
meaning: Operating profit tests whether the business model works before interest and tax. In this game it is EBITDA-like because depreciation is not separately modeled.
higherLower: Positive and improving operating profit usually indicates that the core business can support itself.
simpleExample: $6,000 gross profit − $4,500 operating expenses = $1,500 operating profit.

title: Operating Margin
formula: Operating margin % = Operating profit ÷ Revenue × 100
meaning: Operating margin shows how much operating profit the company keeps from each dollar of revenue.
higherLower: Higher can indicate stronger operating efficiency, but compare businesses with similar models and maturity.

title: Profit Before Tax (PBT)
formula: PBT = EBIT + Investment income + Asset disposal gain/loss − Interest − Legal penalties
meaning: Profit before tax combines operating profit after depreciation with non-operating investment/disposal results and financing/legal costs before income tax.
higherLower: Higher PBT usually means stronger pre-tax profitability; leverage can make PBT much lower than operating profit.
simpleExample: $1,700 EBIT + $100 investment income − $200 interest = $1,600 profit before tax.

title: Tax Accrued
formula: Tax accrued = max(0, PBT) × Tax rate
meaning: Tax accrued is the tax expense recognized for profitable activity even if the cash payment occurs later.
higherLower: A higher tax bill can simply reflect higher profit. The key is planning cash for the liability.
simpleExample: $1,300 taxable profit × 20% tax rate = $260 tax accrued.

title: Net Profit / Loss
formula: Net profit = PBT − Tax accrued
meaning: Net profit is the accounting bottom line after operating costs, interest, penalties and accrued tax.
higherLower: Positive net profit is generally desirable, but one week should not be mistaken for a durable trend.

title: Net Profit Margin
formula: Net margin % = Net profit ÷ Revenue × 100
meaning: Net margin shows how much final profit remains from each dollar of revenue.
higherLower: Higher is usually better, but capital intensity, growth stage and industry structure matter.

title: Change in Cash
formula: Cash change = Ending cash − Previous ending cash
meaning: Cash change measures whether operating cash actually increased or decreased during the week.
higherLower: Positive cash generation improves flexibility. Negative cash can be acceptable temporarily if it funds productive growth.
simpleExample: Cash rises from $20,000 to $23,000, so weekly cash change is +$3,000.

title: Cash Runway
formula: Runway = Cash ÷ Weekly burn
meaning: Runway estimates how many weeks the company could continue if its current loss rate persisted.
higherLower: More runway generally means more time to fix problems or raise capital. It is only an estimate when burn changes rapidly.
simpleExample: $30,000 cash ÷ $3,000 weekly burn = 10 weeks of runway.

title: Inventory Asset
formula: Inventory asset = Inventory units × Average inventory unit cost
meaning: Unsold inventory is normally an asset rather than an immediate expense because it can support future sales.
higherLower: More inventory can protect availability but also traps cash and creates spoilage or obsolescence risk.

title: Total Assets
formula: Total assets = Cash + Reserve + Inventory + Expansion assets + Net PPE + Financial investments
meaning: Assets are resources the company controls that have economic value in the simulation.
higherLower: More assets are useful only if they are productive, liquid enough and financed sensibly.
simpleExample: $20,000 cash + $5,000 reserve + $2,000 inventory + $8,000 expansion assets + $15,000 net PPE + $10,000 investments = $60,000 assets.

title: Total Liabilities
formula: Total liabilities = Debt + Tax payable
meaning: Liabilities are obligations the company must eventually settle.
higherLower: Higher liabilities increase financial obligations; whether they are acceptable depends on earning power and asset quality.

title: Book Equity
formula: Book equity = Total assets − Total liabilities
meaning: Book equity is the accounting residual attributable to owners after subtracting liabilities from assets.
higherLower: Positive equity generally gives a stronger balance-sheet cushion, but book equity is not the same as market valuation.

title: Contribution Margin
formula: Contribution margin % = (Revenue − Variable costs) ÷ Revenue × 100
meaning: Contribution margin shows the percentage of revenue available to pay operating expenses after variable costs.
higherLower: Higher contribution margin lowers the revenue needed to cover fixed and operating expenses.

title: Break-even Revenue
formula: Break-even revenue = Operating expenses ÷ Contribution margin %
meaning: Break-even revenue estimates the sales level needed for contribution profit to cover operating expenses.
higherLower: A lower break-even point generally makes the company easier to sustain, all else equal.
simpleExample: $4,500 operating expenses ÷ 60% contribution margin = $7,500 break-even revenue.

title: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
formula: Simple CAC = Acquisition spend ÷ Paid customers acquired
meaning: CAC measures how much it costs to acquire one customer. The game also uses channel-specific efficiency and competitor effects to produce its effective CAC.
higherLower: Lower CAC is usually better if customer quality and retention are unchanged.

title: Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
formula: Game LTV = Revenue per customer × Unit gross margin ÷ Weekly churn rate
meaning: LTV estimates the gross-profit value expected from a customer over the relationship.
higherLower: Higher LTV is generally better, but it is highly sensitive to churn and margin assumptions.
simpleExample: $20 weekly revenue/customer × 60% margin ÷ 5% churn = about $240 LTV.

title: LTV : CAC
formula: LTV:CAC = Estimated LTV ÷ Effective CAC
meaning: This compares expected customer value with the cost of acquiring that customer.
higherLower: Below 1x suggests value destruction. Around 3x is a common rough benchmark in some recurring-revenue businesses, but it is not universal. Very high values can also mean you are underinvesting in growth.

title: Marketing ROAS
formula: ROAS = Revenue attributed to advertising ÷ Advertising spend
meaning: Return on ad spend measures revenue generated for each advertising dollar.
higherLower: Higher is generally better, but ROAS ignores many costs and should not replace contribution margin or LTV:CAC.

title: Debt : Book Equity
formula: Debt-to-equity = Debt balance ÷ Book equity
meaning: Debt-to-equity measures financial leverage: how much debt is supported by each dollar of accounting equity.
higherLower: Higher leverage can amplify returns and risk. Normal levels differ dramatically across industries.

title: Annualized Current Revenue
formula: Annualized revenue = Current weekly revenue × 52
meaning: Annualizing scales the current week's revenue to a one-year rate. It is a run-rate estimate, not a forecast.
higherLower: Higher annualized revenue can support a higher valuation, but seasonality and one-off sales can make the estimate misleading.

title: Valuation : Revenue Multiple
formula: Valuation / Revenue = Company valuation ÷ Annualized revenue
meaning: This multiple compares estimated company value with annualized revenue.
higherLower: A higher multiple usually requires stronger growth, margins, retention or strategic value. Compare only with similar companies.

title: Company Valuation
formula: Game valuation = Revenue value + Profit value + Customer value − Debt + Selected assets
meaning: Valuation estimates what the operating business may be worth. It is not cash, profit or book equity.
higherLower: A higher valuation is useful only if supported by durable economics; valuation can fall quickly when growth, margins or risk deteriorate.
simpleExample: A company can have $50,000 cash but a $500,000 valuation because buyers value its future earnings and customers.

title: Depreciation Expense
formula: Weekly depreciation = (Asset cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life in weeks
meaning: Depreciation allocates the depreciable cost of a fixed asset across the periods that benefit from using it.
higherLower: Higher depreciation reduces accounting profit, but it is a non-cash expense in the current week. A larger number can simply mean the company owns more depreciable assets.
simpleExample: A $10,000 asset with 5% residual value and 5-year life has $9,500 depreciable amount; $9,500 ÷ 260 weeks ≈ $36.54 weekly depreciation.

title: EBIT
formula: EBIT = EBITDA-like operating profit − Depreciation
meaning: EBIT shows operating profit after recognizing depreciation of fixed assets but before interest and tax.
higherLower: Higher EBIT generally indicates stronger operating profitability after accounting for asset usage.

title: Accumulated Depreciation
formula: Accumulated depreciation = Sum of depreciation recognized since purchase
meaning: Accumulated depreciation is the total portion of an asset's depreciable cost already expensed.
higherLower: It normally rises as assets age. A high balance is not automatically bad; compare it with gross PPE and asset condition.
simpleExample: If a machine records $1,000 depreciation each year for 3 years, accumulated depreciation is $3,000.

title: Net PPE / Fixed Assets
formula: Net PPE = Gross PPE − Accumulated depreciation
meaning: Net PPE is the carrying value of depreciating operating assets on the balance sheet.
higherLower: Higher net PPE can mean more productive capacity, but also more capital tied up in assets.
simpleExample: $50,000 gross equipment − $12,000 accumulated depreciation = $38,000 net PPE.

title: Investment Income
formula: Weekly investment income = Treasury principal × Simulated annual return ÷ 52
meaning: Investment income is the return earned by surplus company cash placed in the game's treasury investments.
higherLower: Higher income is positive, but locking too much cash in investments can reduce operating flexibility.
simpleExample: $10,000 at a simulated 6.5% annual return earns about $12.50 per week before any real-world tax/fees.
